title: Physics of Information Geometry - Part II: Small-Step Active Inference on the Probability Simplex
abstract: This paper is the second in a two-part investigation of the physics of information geometry. While Part I develops a physical foundation for distributional motion on the probability simplex, the present paper studies how that framework manifests in active inference. The treatment is fully self-contained and does not require familiarity with Part I. We focus in particular on active inference through small distributional steps and the geometric structure induced by such local motion. Starting from an initial distribution, an agent evolves its belief state toward a final target distribution through a sequence of constrained updates. We define a relative free energy functional with respect to the preferred distribution and extend it to a relative potential energy analogous to the Helmholtz/Gibbs free-energy decomposition. The evolution is subject to a per-step kinetic constraint expressed through the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between consecutive distributions, which serves as a discrete kinetic energy on the probability simplex. Using the information-geometric Pythagorean theorem on KL balls, we show that sufficiently small local moves dominate large direct jumps, and that greedy maximization of free-energy reduction is globally optimal under the kinetic constraint. This leads to a sequential variational principle in which the optimal trajectory minimizes the associated Lagrangian of the optimization problem. Similar to classical mechanics, the Lagrangian takes on the form as the difference between the kinetic and potential terms, establishing a least-action principle for distributional motion on the simplex. The resulting optimal update admits a closed form as an exponentially tilted version of the current distribution toward the preferred distribution, parametrized by an inverse-temperature-like multiplier. summary: This work develops a geometric framework for understanding how belief states evolve on the probability simplex, treating the process as a physical system governed by a least-action principle. By minimizing an action functional derived from relative free energy and KL divergence, the authors derive the optimal update rule. This shows that optimal inference follows a path analogous to classical mechanics, providing deep connections between information theory and physics.
main_problem: The paper determines the optimal sequence of distributions (path) for an agent to move from an initial belief state to a desired target distribution on the probability simplex.
main_result: The optimal trajectory minimizes an accumulated action functional, leading to a closed-form update where the new distribution is an exponentially tilted version of the current one toward the preferred distribution.
method: It establishes a least-action principle by defining a relative free energy and using the Kullback-Leibler divergence as a discrete kinetic energy constraint.
model_or_system: The system is the belief state evolving on the probability simplex, $\Delta(X)$. The dynamics are governed by minimizing an action functional derived from information geometry.
key_observables: Relative Free Energy, Relative Potential Energy, Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence (as kinetic energy), and the Action Functional.
important_parameters: The step size ($\delta$), which governs the kinetic energy budget, and the Lagrange multiplier ($\lambda_t$) associated with the constraint.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the small-step limit ($\delta 	o 0$) and the application of the information-geometric Pythagorean theorem.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the information-geometric Pythagorean theorem on the probability simplex, showing the optimal step as a projection onto a KL ball, and depict the stopping-time formulation on the 2-simplex.
paper_structure: The paper builds the framework by defining relative free/potential energies, applying the Pythagorean theorem to justify small steps, formulating the problem as minimizing an action functional, and deriving the closed-form, exponentially tilted update rule.
why_interesting: The connection between optimal inference (Free Energy Principle) and classical mechanics (Least Action Principle) provides a powerful, geometric framework for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in complex systems, relevant for modeling open quantum systems or information flow.

The optimal incremental step q⋆ t is the projection of the preferred distribution ppref onto this ball. The resulting decomposition shows that the reduction in free energy is at least as large as the informational step size.
